Not every dog can do this, and not every trainer can or should. With the owners' permission, I used Bishop to help communicate a lesson to Ryder. Dogs naturally understand other dogs better than they understand us. The goal wasn't to make Ryder love every dog she sees-it was to teach her that she doesn't need to react to every dog she sees. Before training, a simple neighborhood walk was nearly impossible. Seeing another dog meant lunging, pulling, and trying to start conflict. Through obedience work and carefully controlled sessions with Bishop, Ryder learned a valuable lesson: not every dog is a threat, and not every situation requires a reaction. Also notice how Bishop's corrections increase in intensity throughout the video. He starts with the minimum amount of pressure necessary and only escalates when Ryder chooses not to listen. That's how dogs naturally communicate with one another. Will I tell these owners to take her to a dog park and expect her to be everyone's best friend? Absolutely not. But can we give her a better quality of life by helping her calmly walk past another dog across the street? Absolutely. Not every dog needs this type of training, but some dogs can benefit tremendously from it. Extra Gooey Cinnamon Rolls (Bakery-Style & No-Knead) Dough * 1 tsp yeast * 2 tbsp sugar * 343 g milk (about 1½ cups) * 480 g flour (about 4 cups + 2 tbsp) * 1 tsp salt * 60 g softened butter (about 4 tbsp) Filling * 140 g softened butter (10 tbsp) * 140 g brown sugar (about ⅔ cup) * 3½ tbsp ground cinnamon Butter Vanilla Frosting * 85 g softened butter (6 tbsp) * 180 g powdered sugar (about 1½ cups) * 1 tbsp vanilla extract Instructions 1. In a bowl, mix the yeast, sugar, and milk. Add the flour and mix until combined. Add the salt and softened butter, then stretch and fold (or coil fold) until the butter is fully incorporated. 2. Cover and let the dough rise for about 2 hours, or until doubled in size. 3. Roll the dough into a large rectangle. Spread the softened butter evenly over the dough, then sprinkle with the brown sugar and cinnamon. 4. Cut the dough into 6 long strips, then roll each strip into a cinnamon roll. 5. Sprinkle a little of the cinnamon sugar mixture into the bottom of the pan, then place the rolls on top. 6. Cover and let them rest for 15 minutes. 7. Mix a little milk with 1 tbsp melted butter, then spoon about 2 tbsp of the mixture over each cinnamon roll. 8. Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 25–30 minutes, or until golden brown. 9. As soon as they come out of the oven, cover them with a clean kitchen towel until warm. Then spread the frosting on top. After 5 weeks of structured behavior work, obedience, and muzzle conditioning, we returned to the same veterinary clinic that Beau struggled in before training. This was a high-stakes moment. There were multiple bite attempts, but here’s the difference: everyone stayed calm, neutral, and communicative. That changed everything. Was it perfect? No. Was Beau safer, more manageable, and able to be treated for a painful bacterial infection in his paw? Yes. Handling a 100+ lb dog with bite history is no small task. Huge respect to my apprentice Kevin and Beau’s owner for staying consistent and showing up when it mattered most.
